title: Breathing advice from Metoyer
summary: Metoyer taught taking breaths at the ends of bars and using the stomach. He always stood up to play, even on jitney dances.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: So far, this sounds like a trumpet lesson. There's one more question I have to ask before we move on to your life again. Did Mr. Matoy ever say anything about breathing, anything special, exercises on breathing or anything that he gave you?

Well, yeah, see, in fact, he taught me from the whole note of breathing at the end of each bar, if you can, that's where you take your breath. Unless you have a break in between the bar where you can take a breath and you're going to have a tie over to the next bar to keep you from turning that tie loose where you'll catch your breath right in between there.
I was thinking in particular like that.

And you can't detect when you're trying to lose because it's done so quick. It's just like automatic grace note in between it that you can't tell if it's, you're doing it accidental or if it's ripped.
I was thinking, did he have any exercises for using your diaphragm rather than just your upper lungs or anything of that kind? Did he ever talk about those things?
Yeah, in breathing, you think about using your stomach in order to throw in full breath

and feel? That's the way he played. That's one system. I don't know whether he did it under his own training or where he was taught, but that's a method he used. He always stood up to play. He meant a jitney dance. He never did sit down to play drunk as long as he'd been playing. Every job he was on, he stood up.
